title: Build to Last — Chris Lattner talks with Jeremy Howard
summary: Chris Lattner and Jeremy Howard argue AI coding helps prototypes and learning but threatens craftsmanship when used to crank out code without understanding.

assertions.quote: it probably is 5 or 10x productivity for prototypes.

verdicts.note: Direction is well supported: greenfield, low-stakes work gets the biggest gains in studies and surveys. The specific multipliers are anecdote.

assertions.quote: it's amazing for learning uh a code base you're not familiar with.

verdicts.note: Agents do speed onboarding and PR summarization, but surveys and the Anthropic learning study show many users skip understanding; outcome depends on use.

assertions.quote: I'm not uh CEO bragging about the number of lines of code written by AI. That's I think a completely useless metric.

verdicts.note: Accepted suggestions are often later rewritten or deleted, and output volume has long been a poor proxy for productivity; controlled studies measure task time or delivery instead.

assertions.quote: unit tests are their own potential tech debt.

verdicts.note: Mock-heavy or change-detector tests do raise maintenance cost, but well-guided AI tests are often useful, so it depends on review.

assertions.quote: It made It made the symptom go away, so it air quote fixed the bug, but it just was so wrong

verdicts.note: Audits of SWE-bench-style patches find many plausible but incorrect or overfitted fixes, though the rate varies by task and model.

assertions.quote: it can end up retarding your development and preventing you from growing and actually getting stuff done.

verdicts.note: Anthropic's 2026 RCT found AI-assisted learners scored lower on mastery of a new library, and other studies show reduced engagement; effects depend on how AI is used.

assertions.quote: the people who do use it to learn more and learn faster are going to like they're going to outpace

verdicts.note: Anthropic's 2026 study found high scorers used AI for conceptual questions and explanations while low scorers delegated; small sample and a single learning task.

assertions.quote: the results were just terrible. We we our productivity fell off a cliff.

verdicts.note: Second-hand anecdote measured by lines of code and commits; controlled and large field studies find average gains of roughly 10-30%, sometimes negative.

assertions.quote: pre-training was a big deal. It seemed exponential but actually it S-curved out and got flat as things went on.

verdicts.note: METR's task-horizon metric kept doubling roughly every 7 months through 2025-26 and coding benchmarks rose sharply; perceived per-release gains feel smaller but the trend is steep.

assertions.quote: I don't like the people that are making decisions as though AGI or ASI were here tomorrow.

verdicts.note: Prediction tracked against 2026 reality: agents handle more scoped tasks, but end-to-end engineering (requirements, review, operations) still depends on people; METR horizons and hiring data don't support 'most or all' yet.

assertions.quote: the people who don't know code being able to get something done that they otherwise couldn't do, that is actually transformative.

verdicts.note: Tools like Lovable, v0, Replit let non-developers produce working prototypes; widely observed.
